GENERAL PREFACE

The teaching of the prophets is generally distorted by the beliefs of the world and the interpretations of the priests. If we wish to ascertain what the founders of great religions taught, we have to get back to the original sources.

Buddhism in all its forms goes back to the life and teaching of the Buddha. While the austerities he practised until attaining enlightenment appeal to the Hinayana, the Pali, or the Southern school, his life of service and compassion for 45 years after attaining enlightenment is the authority for the Mahayana, the Sanskrit or the Northern school.

The religious quest springs from an awareness of the imperfection and suffering of the world. The questions that troubled Tolstoy in the fiftieth year of his life disturb all thinking people: "What is life? Why should I live? Why should I do anything? Is there any meaning in life that can overcome inevitable death?" Nijinsky summed up the whole problem in his Diary when he wrote: "The whole life of my wife and all of mankind is death." How can we be saved from the body of this death? This is the problem of religion.

The Buddha traces suffering to selfish desire. Suffering is the result of tension between a living creature's essential impulse to try to make itself the center of the universe and its essential dependence on the rest of creation. Craving is what binds the individual to the creative process. The individual driven by selfish desire becomes a slave of the universe. We can overcome suffering only if we rid ourselves of tṛṣṇā or tanhā. Attempting to get rid of suffering through various forms of self-deception does not mean ceasing to suffer — it only means suffering in a different way.

The Buddha formulates the eightfold path of morality, which helps us eliminate selfish desire and overcome suffer-

ing. When the Upanishads declare, "That thou art", tat tvam asi, it is not a mere statement of fact. It is a call to action. Make yourself that which you know you can be. Whereas the Hindu mind believes in a permanent element in the individual which can stand firm and unshaken in the midst of change, the Buddhist stresses the dynamic character of the self. No change is possible with an unchanging consciousness. We can achieve the possibilities within us through the exertion of will rather than through the play of intellect. Religion is not a creed, but a vital process. It is no use railing against God or destiny when we ourselves are the authors of our disgrace. If few are chosen, it is because few choose to be chosen. The Buddha laid stress on the creative freedom of humanity. The Buddha did not encourage dependence on the supernatural. He could not conceive of a being capable of creating a world for the express purpose of having its creatures praise him. The ten veramanis or prohibitions or abstinences called dasasila or dasasiksapada which novices on the path of Buddhism recite are given in these words: "I take upon myself the abstinence from: (1) destroying life, (2) taking what is not given, (3) leading an unchaste life, (4) speaking untruth, (5) giving myself to intoxicating drugs, (6) eating at irregular hours, (7) seeing musical and dancing performances and other shows and pageants, (8) wearing garlands, perfumes, unguents and other bodily decorations, (9) using high couches and seats, (10) accepting gifts of gold and silver." The first five constitute the Buddhist pancasila.

I undertake the training rule of abstaining from taking life.
I undertake the training rule of abstaining from taking what is not given.
I undertake the training rule of abstaining from misconduct in sensual pleasures.
I undertake the training rule of abstaining from false speech.
I undertake the training rule of abstaining from distilled and fermented drinks that cause heedlessness.

Conflicts in the world are conflicts in the human soul writ large. If people were at peace within themselves, the outer conflicts between nations would inevitably cease. By practicing the Buddha's pancasila we will develop patience, courage, love

GENERAL PREFACE iii

and unselfishness. The Buddha teaches us that even in an age of anxiety and violence, it is possible to gain and maintain inner harmony, which is not at the mercy of outward circumstance.

Nirvana is the highest bliss. It is not a negative state of annihilation but a positive state of joy, consciousness grown from an unhappy to a beatific one. The Buddha does not tell us that man is but a bubble on the turbulent surface of nature and that he has no destiny save to undergo dissolution. The Hindu affirms that man can realise his identity with Brahman, the ground of all being; the Buddhist says that man can live in a transfigured world where samsara and nirvana are one. In the Maha-saccaka Sutta, the Buddha himself is reported to have described the supreme triumph of reaching the goal of his quest as follows:

"When this knowledge, this insight had arisen within me, my heart was set free from the intoxication of lusts, set free from the intoxication of becomings, set free from the intoxication of ignorance. In me, thus emancipated, there arose the certainty of that emancipation. And I came to know: Rebirth is at an end. The higher life has been fulfilled. What had to be done has been accomplished. After this present life there is no further for this or that. This last insight did I attain in the last watch of the night. Ignorance was beaten down, insight arose, darkness was destroyed, the light came, inasmuch as I was there strenuous, earnest, master of myself." Thus ended the struggle of six long years.

The Buddha is said to be a physician. Just as a physician strives to restore a sick man to health, the Buddha tries to restore us to our normal condition. If our leaders become normal, we may be able to replace the present social order — in which division, falsehood and violence prevail — with a new one in which humanity, truth and brotherhood will reign.

On the occasion of the 2,500th anniversary of the Buddha's passing into final nirvana, the Government of India decided to publish standard versions in Devanagari script of the complete Pali

iv GENERAL PREFACE

and the Sanskrit texts of the two schools, Southern and Northern, in the hope that some of the readers of these books may be impelled to love the good, to practise altruism and hold their spirit aloof from the desires and ambitions of the world.

S. Radhakrishnan

INTRODUCTION

1. The Pāli Tipiṭaka

After the passing away of the Buddha at Kusinārā, the disciples assembled to pay their last respects to him. The Venerable Mahā Kassapa, the chief of the congregation, was offering words of consolation to the grieving assembly, reminding them of the Buddha's own declaration: "It is the very nature of all things near and dear to us that we must be separated from them." However, Subhadra, a monk who had been ordained late in life, did not appear sorrowful. He took a distorted view of the situation and said: "Do not grieve, brothers, for now we are truly free from the restraint of the Great Teacher and his overly strict discipline. While the Teacher was alive, we were constantly rebuked for failing to follow difficult rules; but now we are free to do as we wish — so do not grieve." These words served as a warning about the possible future corruption of the Dhamma at the hands of faithless members of the same type. The Venerable Mahā Kassapa felt an urgent need to convene a Grand Council of the senior Elders of the Saṅgha to make a complete collection of the teachings, and also to establish means for their proper preservation and transmission to future generations. He addressed the monks thus: "Come, friends, let us recite together the Dhamma and the Vinaya...." The Venerable Mahā Kassapa drew up a list of five hundred of the foremost disciples to be appointed as members of the Council. At first, the name of the Venerable Ānanda was omitted, on account of the fact that he had not yet attained Arhathood. But since no one else in the Saṅgha had the privilege of having listened to the Teacher so closely and for such a long period of time, his participation was considered necessary and important. He was therefore asked to go to a suitable place and cultivate insight, in order to attain Arhathood and be able to join the Council in time. King Ajātasattu made the necessary arrangements for the accommodation

vi INTRODUCTION

and convenience of the convention at Rājagaha, a favourite resort of the Teacher himself. A spacious beautiful pavilion was raised for the meeting at the entrance of the Sattapaṇṇi cave, on the northern side of the Vebhāra Hill.

Venerable Ānanda made the best efforts to train himself in developing insight. He kept walking up and down for the whole night absorbed in deep meditation; and, early in the morning, as he was going to stretch himself on the bed, his feet had left the ground and the head had not reached the pillow, at that moment, as if by a flash of light, darkness was dispelled and the sublime light of sainthood dawned upon him. And, through his miraculous superhuman power of an Arhat, he appeared all of a sudden on his appointed seat in the hall, as if emerging out of the ground, exactly as the proceedings were about to begin.

With the permission of the Sangha, Venerable Maha Kassapa questioned Upali on the Vinaya, relating to the different monastic transgressions: the matter, the occasion, the individuals concerned, the principal rules, the amended rules, and all other details about them. In this way, the Vinaya text was agreed upon and settled. Then, again, with the permission of the Sangha, he questioned Ananda on the Dhamma: the occasion of a sermon and the person or persons with reference to whom it was delivered.

The commentary, Atthakatha, of a much later date, assumes that the Abhidhamma Pitaka was also included in the collection of the Dhamma, and that the Tipitaka, as it is available to us, was finalized at this very stage.

A century after the passing away of the Buddha, a great controversy arose in the Sangha concerning the interpretation of some Vinaya rules. This made it necessary to hold the Second Council at Vesali. Seven hundred leading Elders

1. Cullavagga, Chapter XI.     2. Sumangalavilasini, Nidanakatha.

from distant parts of the country assembled to take part in it; and they had drawn up a new edition of the Scripture, resulting in the fixing up of the Piṭakas, Nikāyas, Aṅgas and Dhammakkhandhas.

A century later, when King Asoka embraced Buddhism and extended his patronage to its propagation, the richly furnished monasteries became centers of attraction even for members of other sects. They put on the yellow robe, either through proper ordination or by stealth, and went about as Bhikkhus enjoying the privileges and honor accorded to them. They could not, however, leave their own inclinations behind, and began to twist and distort the Doctrine in their own ways. This led to a state of confusion, and it became difficult to distinguish the true principles from the corrupted ones. The Elders felt the need to safeguard the purity of the Dhamma by carrying out a total purge of alien elements in the philosophical life of the Sangha. This task was entrusted to the Venerable Moggaliputta Tissa, a saint, a thinker, and a writer. He compiled a book called the Kathavatthu, refuting all the foreign theories, which was adopted as part of the Tipitaka at the Third Council held at Pataliputta under his presidency. After the council, Asoka dispatched missionaries to the then civilized parts of the world for the wide propagation of the Dhamma.

Prince Mahinda and Princess Sanghamitta renounced the world and joined the Order to lead a mission to Sihaladipa (Ceylon). From that time on, the island became a stronghold of Buddhism, and even to this day has maintained the tradition of the Pali Tipitaka with all religious zeal.

Up until then, the Tipitaka had been traditionally handed down orally from teachers to pupils. The complete Scripture was compiled in book form for the first time in Ceylon in 29 B.C., under the patronage of King Vattagamani Abhaya, with all the detailed classifications that are now found in the Pali Tipitaka of the Theravada School. This was done

at the Council convened for the purpose, known as the Fourth Great Council.¹

The Fifth Council, according to orthodox tradition, was held at Mandalay, Upper Burma, in 1871, under the patronage of King Mindon. In this Council, the entire Pāli Tipiṭaka was revised, re-edited and finally engraved on 729 marble slabs as follows²:—

Vinaya: 111 slabs
Sutta: 410 slabs
Abhidhamma: 208 slabs

Now, in the present age, the need arose to bring out an up-to-date edition of the Tipiṭaka, printed on modern machines. This task was undertaken by the Burmese Chaṭṭha Saṅgāyana, the Sixth Great Council, held in Rangoon, which opened on 17th May 1954 in an artificially built Rock Cave specially constructed for this purpose, a short distance from the city. Two thousand five hundred of the most learned Bhikkhus from all parts of the world participated in chanting the Tipiṭaka together. A modern printing press was installed in a separate building, and the texts were printed there as soon as they received the approval of the Saṅgāyana. The Council continued functioning for two years and concluded on the full moon day of May 1956, coinciding with the 2500th Jayantī of the Buddha.

In Ceylon, Burma, Thailand and Cambodia the principal religion of the people is Theravāda Buddhism, which adheres to the Pāli Tipiṭaka as its Scripture. There, editions of it have been published in their own scripts. The Pali Text Society, London, has managed to complete the publication of a major portion of it in Roman characters. But even so, it is not yet fully available in any script of India.

It is with a view to filling this gap that the Government of India and the State Government of Bihar have jointly

1. Mahāvaṃsa, Chapters X–XXIII. 2. Buddhist Dharma in 2500 Years, 1956, p. 35.

sanctioned a scheme of editing and publishing the entire Pāli Tipiṭaka in Devanāgarī, which will be complete in 40 volumes of about 400 pages each. This task has been entrusted to the Devanāgarī Tripiṭaka Publication Department, Nalanda. It aims at presenting a co-ordinated edition of the text based on the printed books in Roman, Sinhalese, Burmese and Siamese scripts.

The following chart will show the distribution of books in the literature:

Therīgāthā, x. Jātaka, xi. Niddesa, xii. Paṭisambhidāmagga, xiii. Apadāna, xiv. Buddhavaṃsa, and xv. Cariyāpiṭaka

x INTRODUCTION

2. The Present Volume

In this volume we are publishing the following five books of the Khuddaka Nikāya of the Sutta Piṭaka — the Khuddakapāṭha, Dhammapada, Udāna, Itivuttaka, and Suttanipāta. These are rather more collections of stanzas and passages drawn from various books of the Tipiṭaka than independently composed compilations. The Khuddakapāṭha is almost entirely in stanzas, and the Dhammapada is fully so. The main body of the Udāna is in prose, with a concluding utterance by the Buddha or a disciple at the end, generally in stanzas. The Itivuttaka and the Suttanipāta are written in a mixed style of prose and poetry. We provide below a short introduction to each of these:

1. THE KHUDDAKAPĀṬHA

This is the smallest book in the entire Tipiṭaka, a collection of nine short pieces. It appears to have been compiled for the use of beginning students of the Doctrine. It opens with taking refuge in the Triple Gem — the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Sangha. This is followed by the ten precepts of the novice monk (Sāmaṇera): I take the vow of refraining from taking life, from stealing, from sexual indulgence, from falsehood, from intoxicants, from eating at improper times, from dance, song, music, and witnessing exciting performances, from the use of garlands, perfumes, and cosmetics, from the use of high and luxurious beds, and from accepting gold or silver.

Next comes the important meditation on the impurities of the body, the Kāyagatā Sati — "There are in this body dirty things, such as hairs, nails, teeth, skin, bones, urine, and brain pulp in the skull."

The following piece is called the Kumāra-pañhā, or the Juvenile Queries, in which ten questions are posed and answered, as follows:

What is one? That which all beings live on — food.
What are two? Mind and body.
What are three? The three feelings.

INTRODUCTION xi

What are four? The Four Noble Truths.
What are five? The Five Aggregates of Attachment.
What are six? The six bases pertaining to the self.
What are seven? The seven factors conducive to the attainment of Enlightenment.
What are eight? The Eightfold Noble Path.
What are nine? The nine states of existence.
What are ten? The ten requisite factors for being an Arhat.

The next two suttas — the Mangala Sutta and the Ratana Sutta — have been taken from the Suttanipata. In Buddhist countries, the recitation of these texts is considered very auspicious.

The Tirokudda Sutta describes spirits who are always eager to receive the merit offered in their names by their relatives. A spirit says: "We neither raise cattle nor engage in trade or farming, but we live on the gifts made by our relatives in our names. Just as rain falling from above flows downward, so the gifts given here are received by the departed."

The Nidhikanda Sutta teaches that all worldly wealth and riches are transitory and unreliable; only the merit a person accumulates in this world accompanies him into the next.

The ninth and final Sutta, the Metta Sutta, is one of the most important texts in the entire Tipitaka. It serves as a basis for meditation on universal loving kindness, which the Buddha so greatly emphasized.

2. THE DHAMMAPADA

The book contains 423 stanzas in all, grouped into 26 Vaggas. In Buddhist countries it holds the same prominent place in the common religious life of the people as the Gita does in India. They are even very similar in size and form. The Dhammapada has rightly been called the "Gita of the Buddhists." We present below some specimen extracts from the book —

This page is an introduction summarizing the key themes of various chapters (Vaggas) from the Dhammapada:

Yamaka Vagga: Hatred is never overcome by hatred, but by love — this is an eternal truth. Sinful people suffer both in this life and the next, grieving even more when they reflect on their wrongdoings. The virtuous, by contrast, rejoice in both lives, feeling ever greater happiness at their good deeds. A person may be widely read, but if they do not live by what they know, they are no better than a cowherd counting someone else's cattle.

Citta Vagga: The mind is restless and unstable. Controlling it is hard. The wise, however, train it to be calm and obedient.

Bala Vagga: If, as you go through life, you find no one equal or superior to yourself, it is better to travel alone — there is nothing to be gained from the company of a fool.

Pandita Vagga: One who corrects and guides others away from wrongdoing is treasured by the good, though resented by the bad. In truth, few people genuinely seek to reach the other shore; most merely pace back and forth along this one.

Arhanta Vagga: Even the gods admire the person who has mastered the senses as a charioteer masters horses, and who has shed egotism and inner impurity.

Papa Vagga: Neither in the sky, nor in the ocean's depths, nor in mountain caves — nowhere can one escape the consequences of evil deeds.

Danda Vagga: All beings fear punishment; all dread death. Recognizing others as like oneself, one should neither kill nor incite killing.

Jara Vagga: When everything is burning, what cause is there for laughter and joy? You are shrouded in darkness, yet you do not seek a lamp.

Atta Vagga: One is one's own master — who else could be? When a person conquers themselves, they achieve a mastery that is truly rare.

INTRODUCTION xiii

Buddha Vagga. To refrain from evils, to do good, to purify the mind — this is the teaching of the Buddhas.

Sukha Vagga. We live happily, with love, among those who hate. We dwell free from enmity among those who are full of it. The victor breeds feelings of enmity; the vanquished suffers a disturbed sleep. The Liberated One, risen above the consideration of victory and defeat, is blissful. To be free from disease is a great gain, contentment is the best wealth, trust is the true relative, and Nibbāna is the highest attainment.

Kodha Vagga. He alone is a true charioteer who can hold himself back from going astray in anger. Those otherwise called charioteers are mere holders of reins. Let one conquer evil by goodness, a miser by generosity, and falsehood by truth.

Brāhmaṇa Vagga. One is never a Brāhmaṇa by wearing knotted hair, nor by family, nor by birth. He alone is truly a Brāhmaṇa who is endowed with truth, piety, and purity.

3. THE UDĀNA

The word "Udāna" means an utterance that a saint breathes forth in the bliss of his emancipation or in appreciation of a sublime state. The book bearing this name is a collection of Suttas containing such utterances of the Buddha or of his chief disciples. The following is an introduction to some of these —

Saṅgāmaji Sutta. The former wife of Bhikkhu Saṅgāmaji heard that he had arrived at Sāvatthi. She brought their child before him and said — "This is your child. Take care of it." At this, the Bhikkhu remained silent, not even looking toward her. When she saw that he was not interested in either her or the child, she left the place in utter disappointment. The Bhikkhu remained unmoved.

The Blessed One observed this with his superhuman sight and uttered —

"He does not greet her as she approaches, nor does he worry as she departs. Saṅgāmaji is free from attachment. Him I call a Brāhmaṇa."

Khu. 1—Kha

This page is already in English and requires no translation. It is the introduction (page xiv) to a volume, summarizing two suttas:

The Nanda Sutta describes how Bhikkhu Nanda, a cousin of the Buddha, struggled with monastic life because he was still attached to his beloved Janapada-kalyāṇī. The Buddha used his supernatural power to take Nanda to the realm of the gods, where they encountered celestial nymphs of extraordinary beauty. When Nanda admitted that compared to these nymphs, Janapada-kalyāṇī seemed as plain as a burned, noseless monkey, the Buddha promised to win those nymphs for him if he committed himself fully to the spiritual path. Nanda practiced earnestly in seclusion and eventually attained sainthood — Arahantship — and lost all desire for the nymphs. The Buddha then proclaimed: "One who has crossed the mire, crushed the thorns of desire, ended all delusion, and remains unmoved by pain or pleasure — that person is truly a Bhikkhu."

The Nānātitthiya Sutta recounts how followers of various religious sects argued with one another, each insisting their own doctrine was the truth. To illustrate the folly of this, the Buddha told the story of a king who gathered all the blind people of his kingdom and had them touch an elephant. Each person described the elephant differently based on the part they had touched — a leg felt like a pillar, a tusk like a smooth sharp peg — and they all quarreled, insisting their own description was correct.

INTRODUCTION xv

The Buddha declared: "These wandering ascetics and priests, with their own limited vision, stubbornly cling to their own views and quarrel among themselves."

4. THE ITIVUTTAKA

The name means "It has been thus said." All the discourses in this book open with the declaration: "This has been said by the Blessed One, this has been said by the Liberated One — so I have heard." It is perhaps because of this style that the book received this name. It contains four Nipātas, or collections, dealing with principles grouped in ones, twos, threes, and fours, as follows:

Lobha Sutta (Discourse on Greed). This has been said by the Blessed One, this has been said by the Liberated One — so I have heard.

"Monks, give up one thing. I assure you that you will attain the state of a Non-Returner. What one thing? Monks, it is Greed. Give it up. I assure you that you will attain the state of a Non-Returner."

The Blessed One said this. And it has been said: "The wise give up greed, knowing full well that it leads people into states of misery. They abandon it and never return to this world."

This was said by the Blessed One — so I have heard.
Sīla Sutta (Discourse on Virtue). This has been said by the Blessed One, this has been said by the Liberated One — so I have heard.

"Monks, a person who has two things is destined for hell. Which two? Wrong conduct and wrong view. Monks, a person who has these two is destined for hell." The Blessed One said this. And it has been said:

"Wrong conduct and wrong view —
one who possesses these two
is reborn in hell after death."

This was said by the Blessed One — so I have heard.
Vedanā Sutta (Discourse on Feeling). This has been said by the Blessed One, this has been said by the Liberated One — so I have heard.

xvi INTRODUCTION

"Monks, there are three feelings. Which three? Pleasant, painful, and neither pleasant nor painful. Monks, these are the three feelings."

The Blessed One said this. It has been said:

"The monk who is concentrated, mindful, and aware knows the states of feeling and also their origin. He also knows where they cease, and the path leading to that cessation. Through the cessation of feelings, he is known as the Liberated One."

This was said by the Blessed One — thus I have heard.

Tanhuppāda Sutta. This has been said by the Blessed One, this has been said by the Freed One — thus I have heard.

"Monks, there are four things to which a monk may become attached. What four things? Monks, a monk may become attached to a robe, to alms, to an abode, or to other things."

The Blessed One said this. It has been said:

"Due to attachment, a being
wanders on and on,
and is not freed from the world.
Seeing this evil in attachment,
the cause of all misery,
let the monk be alert
and rid himself of attachment and craving."

The Blessed One said this — thus I have heard.

5. THE SUTTA NIPĀTA

The Suttanipāta is one of the most important books in the Khuddaka Nikāya. Its language and style are considered to be close to those of the Vedas. Its last two chapters — the Atthaka Vagga and the Pārāyana Vagga — are so important that the commentary written on them, the Niddesa, has been incorporated into the collection of this Nikāya. Some of the Suttas are written entirely in verse and some are in a mixed style of prose and poetry. The following is an introduction to some of them:

Khaggavisāna Sutta. This Sutta gives an account of the

INTRODUCTION xvii

ideals of a Pacceka Buddha. Having shunned all, he dwells all alone. He has been compared to the horn of a rhinoceros, as —

Not doing harm to any being, not inflicting pain on anyone, let one not wish for son or friend. Better to dwell all alone, like the horn of the rhinoceros.

Having given up greed, ill will and delusion, having destroyed all fetters, not being daunted even by death, let one dwell all alone, like the horn of the rhinoceros.

Kasibhāradvāja Sutta. The Brāhmaṇa Bhārdvāja chides the Buddha — "O recluse, I till and sow. Having tilled and sown, I eat. Let you too till and sow."

The Buddha said — "O Brāhmaṇa, I also till and sow. I also eat having tilled and sown."

The Brāhmaṇa said — "I do not see with you either oxen or plough or other agricultural implements. Then, how can you say that you till and sow?"

The Buddha gave a spiritual explanation of it, saying — "Faith is the seed, penance is the rain, wisdom is the ox and plough, mind is the reins,... and the product of this cultivation is deathlessness, Nibbāna."

This opened the eyes of the Brāhmaṇa. He accepted the discipleship of the Buddha. He was duly ordained. He attained to the state of sainthood, Arahantship.

Vasala Sutta. The Brāhmaṇa Aggika Bhāradvāja reviled the Buddha, calling him a Vasala, an outcaste. The Buddha gave him a sermon on who is truly an outcaste, in which he demolished the principles of caste distinctions. He said —

"It is not by birth, but by action that one is truly an outcaste or a Brāhmaṇa."

Metta Sutta. This sutta is used for the practice of meditation on universal loving kindness. Even the recitation of this sutta is regarded as very auspicious by Buddhists. The meaning of the Sutta is as follows —

The wise man, seeking the attainment of the Sublime, should be capable, upright, exceedingly upright, gentle, humble,

contented, of few wants, of few duties, of simple livelihood, calm in the senses, clever, docile and without greed. He must not do even the smallest thing that might cause the wise to speak ill of him.

May all beings be happy. All beings — those that move and those that do not, those that are big and those that are small — may they be happy. Let one extend to all the same feelings of love that a mother has towards her only son. While walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, as long as one does not fall asleep, one should maintain the same feeling of loving kindness toward all. This is called Brahma-Vihara. Not falling into wrong views, being pure in life, endowed with insight, having conquered attachment to worldly pleasures, one must not return to the womb of a mother.

Ratana Sutta. In Buddhist countries the recitation of this sutta is considered to have miraculous effects in warding off ill omens and evil influences. The verses praise the great merits of the Buddha, Dhamma, and Sangha, and thereby invoke their blessings for the well-being of all.

Mangala Sutta. The Buddha teaches a certain god that the highest blessings consist in the following: not living with fools, associating with the wise, worshipping worthy persons, dwelling in a suitable place, having merits from previous actions, following the right path, being learned, knowing the arts, being disciplined, serving one's parents, providing for wife and children, having orderly conduct, giving gifts, being righteous, looking after one's family and relatives, avoiding and shunning evils, refraining from intoxicants, and so on.

Brahmanadhammika Sutta. This sutta gives an account of the virtues of the Brahmanas of old and the failings of those of the present day. Devotion to the cow is emphasized. The Buddha says: "The cow is essential to our well-being, just as are the mother, father, brother, and other relatives. She is the giver of food, strength, beauty, and happiness. All manner of evils arose when the Brahmanas began to sacrifice cows. At first there were only three diseases — desire, hunger, and aging. Due to the sin of cow-sacrifice, their number rose to ninety-eight."

PREFACE

1. The Pali Tipitaka

After the passing away of the Buddha at Kushinagar, his disciples gathered together to offer their individual tributes of reverence. At that time, Ayushman Mahakassapa, the leader of the Sangha, consoled everyone by reminding them of the Buddha's teaching: "All things are impermanent, and separation from them is inevitable." In that assembly there was also an elderly ordained monk named 'Subhadda', who, rather than being sorrowful at the Buddha's passing, expressed gladness and said: "O monks, do not grieve. We are now freed from the strict control of that great ascetic. He would constantly say, 'This you must do, and this you must not.' Now we shall do whatever we wish and shall not do what we do not wish. So please, do not be sad."

These words of 'Subhadda' served as a warning, and Ayushman Mahakassapa felt the urgent need to convene a meeting of the leading monks, in which the authentic collection of the Buddha's words could be compiled, so that the Dhamma might be preserved and its tradition could pass unimpeded to future generations. He therefore addressed the monks: "Friends, let us recite the Dhamma and Vinaya together." He prepared a list of suitable monks to participate in this assembly. Initially he did not include the name of Ayushman Ananda, because Ananda had not yet attained the status of Arahant. However, no one else in the entire Sangha had been as fortunate as Ayushman Ananda in having remained in the closest contact with the Blessed One and in having heard his words directly. So in the end, Ayushman Mahakassapa had to include his name as well. Ayushman Ananda then devoted himself with complete faith and energy to meditative practice, so that he might attain the state of Arahantship before the date of the assembly.

The then king of Magadha, Ajatashatru, had a large and beautiful pavilion constructed at the entrance to the 'Sattapanni' cave located on the northern slope of the 'Vebhara' mountain near Rajagriha, and it was here that the said assembly of monks commenced.

Meanwhile, Ayushman Ananda also achieved success in his effort. Throughout the night he remained absorbed in meditation, walking back and forth. In the morning, just as he sat down to lie on his bed, his feet had already left the ground and his head had not yet reached the pillow, when in that very moment, the darkness of his ignorance was dispelled and the light of supreme knowledge arose within him. He attained the state of Arahantship —
Khu. 1 – ga

( 2 )

he had settled in. By his divine power, at the very moment the session began, he took his designated seat in the assembly hall as though he had arisen from the very womb of the earth.

With the permission of the Sangha, the Venerable Mahakassapa asked Upali about the rules of the Vinaya, and the Venerable Upali gave the Sangha a detailed answer to those questions. Then, in the same manner, the Venerable Mahakassapa asked Ananda about the Dharma taught by the Blessed One, the Buddha, to which he gave a complete reply. In this way both the 'Vinaya' and the 'Dhamma' were compiled.¹ However, in the 'Atthakatha literature' written several centuries after this council, it is mentioned that at this very first session the 'Abhidhamma Pitaka' was also compiled, and that the 'Tipitaka' literature as we have it today was composed at that time in the very form in which we now possess it.²

A century after the Buddha's Nirvana, a great dispute arose over the rules of the Vinaya, and to resolve it, a second session was convened at Vaishali. Seven hundred renowned monks, chosen from the far-flung regions of the country, participated in it. For this reason, this second council is known as the 'Saptashatika' (Council of Seven Hundred).³

A hundred years after this, when Emperor Ashoka embraced Buddhism and it received royal patronage, others of different persuasions, seeing the advantage, were also drawn toward Buddhist monasteries. Taking formal ordination or simply donning yellow robes quietly, they began to live in the monasteries calling themselves Buddhist monks. But it was not easy for them to give up their old habits and ideas. Consequently, they began to interpret the Dharma in their own ways, distorting it as they pleased. As a result, an unruliness appeared in the intellectual life of the monastic Sangha and it became difficult to determine the true nature of the Dharma. The elder monks who were the guardians of the Dharma felt the need for a third council, in order to preserve the purity of the Dharma permanently and to keep it free from opposing elements. This council was held under the leadership of Emperor Ashoka's teacher, the Venerable Moggaliputta Tissa, at the monastery called 'Ashokarama' in Pataliputra. The Venerable Tissa, refuting the impure doctrines and expounding the authentic tradition of the pure 'Sthaviravada' school, composed a work called 'Kathavatthu,' which the Sangha at the third council honoured with the status of the Buddha's own word. To this day it is considered a priceless work of 'Tipitaka literature.' After this council, Ashoka sent out missionaries to spread the Dharma to distant lands.⁴

People were feeling the need that in this modern age the most beautiful printed edition of the Tipitaka should be published using the latest technology. It was decided that this need would be fulfilled through the Sixth Council (Chattha Sangayana) to be held in Burma. In a beautifully constructed stone cave not far from the capital Rangoon, the session of the council commenced on 17 May, 1954. Two thousand five hundred learned monks invited from various countries of the world participated in the council. The original Tipitaka accepted by the council was printed there at its own press. The session of the council concluded on the day of the twenty-five-hundredth Buddha Jayanti in 1956 CE.

In Lanka, Burma, Thailand, Cambodia and other countries, the state religion is Buddhist Theravada, whose universally accepted scripture is the Pali Tipitaka. In those countries, beautiful editions of the Tipitaka in their respective scripts have been published from time to time. The Pali Text Society of London has also published most of the Tipitaka in Roman script. However, until now this invaluable literature has not been available in any script of India.

2. The Present Work

This volume contains a collection of these five texts from the Khuddakanikaya of the Suttapitaka — the Khuddakapatha, Dhammapada, Udana, Itivuttaka and Suttanipata. It does not appear that these five were composed independently. Most of their portions have been gathered from various texts of the Tripitaka. The Khuddakapatha and Dhammapada consist entirely of verses; the main body of the Udana's suttas is in prose and the udana itself usually comes at the end in verse; and the Suttanipata and Itivuttaka are written in a mixed style of prose and verse. Their introduction is as follows:—

1. Khuddakapatha

This is the smallest text in the entire Tripitaka. It is a collection of nine short lessons. It appears that this was compiled with the intention of being read by beginners in the Dhamma.

The text begins with the taking of refuge in the Buddha, Dhamma and Sangha. Then the ten training rules for a novice (shramanera) are mentioned — I take the vow to abstain from taking life, from theft..., from unchastity..., from false speech..., from the use of intoxicants..., from eating at improper times..., from watching dancing, singing and indecent gestures..., from using garlands, perfumes and the like..., from sleeping on high and luxurious beds..., and I take the vow to abstain from receiving gold and silver.

After this, the method of the 'Kayagata Sati' (mindfulness of the body) contemplation is described, in which one reflects on the thirty-two impurities of one's own body — in this body there are hair of the head, body hair, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinew, bone, marrow, and so on.

The heading of the next lesson is 'Kumarapañha' (Questions for Youths), in which ten questions are asked and answered, such as —

What is one thing? All beings subsist on food.
What are two things? Name and form.
What are three things? Three feelings.
What are four things? The four noble truths.
What are five things? The five aggregates of clinging.
What are six things? The six internal sense bases.
What are seven things? The seven factors of enlightenment.
What are eight things? The noble eightfold path.
What are nine things? The nine realms of living beings.
What are ten things? The ten things possessed by one who becomes an arahant.

The two suttas that follow, the 'Mangalasutta' and the 'Ratasutta,' are taken from the Suttanipata. In Buddhist countries, their recitation is considered of great importance.

The 'Tirokududasutta' describes departed spirits who yearn for the memorial offerings made by their relatives. It is told through the mouths of the spirits: "We neither keep cattle, nor do we farm, nor

( 6 )

commerce. Our relatives, by performing acts of charity and merit directed toward us, sustain us. Just as rainwater falling from above flows down and reaches the lower level, so too does the charity given in this world reach the departed spirits.

The 'Nidhikanda-sutta' demonstrates that all the treasures of the world are perishable; only the merit earned by a person accompanies him into the next world.

The ninth sutra of the text is of great importance. Based on it, the practice of 'Maitri Brahma-vihara Bhavana' (meditation on loving-kindness) is carried out.

2. Dhammapada

It contains a total of 26 chapters and 423 verses. Buddhist countries hold this book in the same reverence and devotion as India holds the 'Gita.' Both are similar in form and nature as well. A certain scholar rightly gave the Dhammapada the name 'Buddhist Gita.' Its verses are as follows:—

Yamakavagga — Hatred is not appeased by hatred; it is appeased only by love — this is the ancient law. Here one grieves, and after death one grieves; the sinful person grieves in both places; seeing his own evil deeds, he is troubled and distressed. Here one rejoices, and after death one rejoices; the virtuous person rejoices in both places; seeing his own good deeds, he is glad and delighted. Though a person may recite many scriptures, if he does not act accordingly, he is like a cowherd who merely counts the cattle of others.

Cittavagga — The mind is fickle and unsteady; it is hard to control. The wise person straightens it.

Balavagga — While wandering through the world, if one does not find a companion equal to or better than oneself, one should travel alone. There is no benefit in the company of fools.

Panditavagga — One who, by giving counsel, restrains others from wrongdoing, is dear to the virtuous and disliked by the wicked. Very few are those who truly wish to cross over to the other shore; most merely run back and forth along the bank.

Arahantavagga — Even the gods envy that holy person who has brought his senses under control just as a skilled charioteer controls horses, and whose pride and mental impurity have departed.

Papavagga — Neither in the sky, nor in the middle of the ocean, nor in the caves of mountains — nowhere in this world can a person go to escape from the consequences of evil deeds.

Dandavagga — All fear punishment; all dread death. Recognizing others as like oneself, one should neither kill nor cause to be killed.

Jaravagga — When fire is constantly burning, what room is there for laughter and delight? Covered in darkness, you do not even seek a lamp!

Attavagga — A person is his own master. How can anyone else be his master? When he conquers himself, he attains a rare and priceless sovereignty.

( 7 )

Buddhavagga — To refrain from all evil, to do good, to purify one's own mind — this is the teaching of the Buddhas.

Sukhavagga — We live in happiness — with love among those who hate. Among hostile people we dwell free from hatred. Victory breeds enmity; the defeated one suffers; and the person who is at peace, free from the notion of victory and defeat, lives in happiness. Good health is a great gain, contentment is the greatest wealth, trust is the greatest companion, and Nirvana is the supreme happiness.

Kodhavagga — Only that person can truly be called a charioteer who restrains the surge of anger, like a runaway chariot. Others merely hold the reins. Conquer the wicked with goodness, conquer the miser with generosity, and conquer the liar with truth.

Brahmanavagga — It is not by matted hair, nor by lineage, nor by birth that one becomes a brahmin. Truly, a brahmin is one who possesses truth, righteousness, and purity.

3. Udana

The word 'Udana' means — a spontaneous utterance of joy that flows from the lips of saints. This book is a collection of such utterances, divided into eight sections of ten suttas each. The style of the suttas is generally uniform. First comes a prose narrative describing the occasion that prompted the utterance of the Udana words, and at the end the Udana itself is usually rendered in verse. By way of example, a few suttas are introduced as follows —

Sanghamajisutta — The former wife of the monk Sanghamajit heard that he had arrived in Shravasti. Taking her children in her arms, she went to him and said: "Monk, this is your child — please look after him." The monk remained silent. The woman set the child down on the ground before him and left. She went ahead, hid herself, and began to watch what the monk would do. Sanghamajit sat quietly on his seat, absorbed in meditation. Seeing this, she returned, picked up the child, and went away disappointed. The Blessed One saw this with his divine sight. From his lips these words of Udana spontaneously arose —

"He welcomes not what comes, nor grieves for what has gone. Sanghamajit is free from attachment. Him do I call a brahmin."

Nandasutta — Nanda was the Lord Buddha's cousin. Under pressure he had taken up the life of a monk, but his mind remained deeply attached to Janapada-kalyani. Buddha came to know of this. To bring him to the right path, Buddha devised a plan. Using his supernatural power, he took Nanda and appeared in the world of the gods. There, Indra came to welcome them, accompanied by a retinue of celestial nymphs. Buddha asked Nanda: "Nanda, are these nymphs more beautiful, or your Janapada-kalyani?"

"Venerable One, compared to these nymphs, Janapada-kalyani would be like a noseless, scorched monkey!"

"Very well then, Nanda — I assure you that if you accomplish the path I have shown you, I will give you these nymphs."

( 8 )

The monk Nanda, driven by desire for the celestial nymphs, threw himself with great enthusiasm into the practice of yoga. He attained perfection. He became an Arahant, free of craving. At that point, what use was the lure of celestial nymphs to him! Seeing this, words of uplift (udana) fell from the Buddha's lips:

"One who has crossed the mud,
who has crushed the thorn of sensual desire,
who has attained the destruction of delusion,
and who is not disturbed by pleasure or pain — that one is a true monk."

Nanaditthiya Sutta — At that time, ascetics of many different views had gathered and were debating among themselves — "This is the Dhamma, this is not." Seeing this, the Buddha told the monks a story:

A king showed an elephant to some blind men and asked them what an elephant is like. The blind man who had grasped the elephant's leg said, "Sire, an elephant is like a pillar." The one who had grasped its ear said, "Sire, an elephant is like a winnowing fan." The one who had grasped its tusk said, "Sire, an elephant is like a peg," and so on. They began arguing among themselves — "An elephant is like this, not like that."

The Buddha compared those ascetics of many views to these very blind men, who argue because each has only partial knowledge of the truth. Words of uplift fell from his lips:

"Some ascetics and brahmins, having seen only one part, insist on it and quarrel with one another."

4. Itivuttaka

The word 'Itivuttaka' means "Thus it was said." This text is a collection of 112 discourses of the Buddha. All its suttas begin in this manner: "The Blessed One said this, the Arahant said this — thus have I heard." It is probably because of this style of beginning each sutta that the text came to be called 'Itivuttaka.'

The text is divided into four Nipatas. Suttas dealing with one topic are placed in the 'Ekaka-nipata'... and suttas dealing with four topics are placed in the 'Catukka-nipata.' For example:

Lobha Sutta — The Blessed One said this, the Arahant said this — thus have I heard.
"O monks! Abandon one thing; I give you my assurance of attaining the state of non-return (anagami). What is that one thing?

"O monks, abandon the one thing that is greed. I give you my assurance of attaining the state of non-return. This the Blessed One said. Thus it is proclaimed:

"People who fall into greed reach a bad destination;
wise people, understanding that greed well, abandon it;
and having abandoned it, they never again
return to this world."
This too was said by the Blessed One — thus have I heard.

( 9 )

Soḷasutta — Thus has the Blessed One said, thus has the Arahant said — so have I heard.
"Monks, a person endowed with two things will fall into hell. Which two? Bad conduct and bad views. Monks, a person endowed with these two things will fall into hell."
Thus spoke the Blessed One. It is said —
"One who is endowed with bad conduct and bad views —
such a person, lacking wisdom, dies and is reborn in hell."
This too was said by the Blessed One. So have I heard.

Vedanāsutta — Thus has the Blessed One said, thus has the Arahant said — so have I heard.
"Monks, there are three kinds of feeling. Which three? Pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-pleasant-nor-painful feeling — monks, these are the three feelings." Thus spoke the Blessed One. It is said —
"The monk who is composed, fully aware, and mindful knows the feelings and their origin. He knows where they cease and the path leading to that cessation.
With the ending of feelings, he is called accomplished and fully quenched."
This too was said by the Blessed One. So have I heard.

Taṇhuppādasutta — Thus has the Blessed One said, thus has the Arahant said — so have I heard.
"Monks, there are four grounds for the arising of craving in a monk. Which four? Monks, craving arises in a monk on account of robes, on account of alms-food, on account of lodging, and on account of various other things."
Thus spoke the Blessed One. It is said —
"A person wandering long with craving is not freed from the snare of the world.
Seeing this danger in craving as the cause of suffering, let the monk remain vigilant and go forth, freed from craving and clinging."
This too was said by the Blessed One. So have I heard.

5. Suttanipāta

Among the texts of the Khuddakanikāya, the Suttanipāta holds great importance. Its language and style are compared to those of the Vedas. Its last two sections — the Aṭṭhakavagga and the Pārāyanavagga — are considered so significant that the commentary written on them, the Niddesa, has been accorded the honor of being a canonical Tipiṭaka text. Some of its suttas are entirely in verse, while others are mixed prose and verse. Summaries of a few suttas are given below as examples:—

Dhaniyasutta — Dhaniya the cowherd householder, blessed with all comforts, is expressing feelings of contentment and joy. On the other side, the Blessed One, the Buddha, sitting in the open sky on the bank of the Mahī river, being free from craving, is expressing the joy of his liberation. Dhaniya the cowherd, filled with devotion, goes to the Blessed One, pays his respects, and surrenders himself to the Three Refuges.

Khu. 1—Gha

( 10 )

Khaggavisana Sutta — This sutta describes the conduct of a Pratyeka-Buddha (solitary enlightened one). He abandons all bonds and lives alone in solitude. His simile is that of the rhinoceros horn. As it is said —

Laying down the rod toward all living beings, harming none,
let him not desire a son, nor a companion.
Let him wander alone, like the horn of the rhinoceros.
Crushing all bonds, casting off passion, hatred, and delusion,
undaunted even by death, let him wander alone
like the horn of the rhinoceros.

Kasibharadvaja Sutta — The brahmin Bharadvaja scolds the Blessed One Buddha, saying: "O recluse, I plough, I harrow, I eat after ploughing and harrowing. You too should plough and harrow, and eat after doing so."

Buddha replied: "I too farm. I too plough and harrow, and eat after ploughing and harrowing."

The brahmin said: "I see no oxen, no plough, and no other farming implements of yours. How then do you say that you farm?"

Explaining his spiritual farming, Buddha said: "Faith is the seed, austerity is the rain, wisdom is the ox and the plough, the yoke-pin is [conscience], the mind is the reins, mindfulness is the ploughshare and goad..."

The brahmin's eyes were opened. He took refuge as a disciple. And, going forth into homelessness, he attained the rank of Arahant.

Vasala Sutta — The brahmin 'Aggika Bharadvaja' drove Buddha away, calling him a vrsala (outcast). Buddha gave a teaching on who truly is an outcast, in which he refuted caste-ism. He said: By birth no one is an outcast, nor a brahmin; it is by one's actions that one becomes an outcast or a brahmin.

Understanding arose in the brahmin. He took refuge as a disciple.

Metta Sutta — This sutta is of great importance for the practice of loving-kindness (metta) meditation. In Buddhist countries, people consider the recitation of this sutta highly auspicious. The meaning of the sutta is as follows —

One who wishes to attain the peaceful state of Nirvana should be capable, upright, very upright, easy to speak to, gentle, without conceit, content, easily supported, having few duties, living lightly, with calm faculties, skilled, not bold or forward, not greedy. One should not do even the smallest thing for which wise people would criticize another.

May all living beings dwell happily. However many beings there are — those who move and those who do not move, tall, large, medium, small, subtle, gross, seen, unseen, those dwelling far or near, those born or yet to be born — may all be happy.

Let no one deceive another or despise anyone anywhere; let no one through anger or ill-will wish harm upon another. Just as a mother would protect her only child with her own life, so too let him cultivate a boundless mind toward all living beings. Let him radiate love in all directions, above, below, and around. Whether standing, walking, sitting, or lying down — as long as he is awake — let him maintain this state of mind. This is called the brahma-vihara. Freed from wrong views, virtuous, endowed with wisdom, having conquered craving for sensual pleasures, one will never again be reborn in a womb.

( 11 )

Ratanasutta — This sutta is considered of great importance in Buddhist countries. It is recited in various ways by monks for the pacification of inauspiciousness. It contains praise of the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Sangha, and invokes their authority as a blessing. The entire sutta is in verse. Almost every verse ends with — "In the Buddha, Dhamma, or Sangha this is the supreme jewel; by this truth may there be well-being." One verse runs as follows: "The old is worn out, no new one arises. Their minds are not attached to a future birth; their seeds are gone, their desires do not grow. These wise ones attain Nirvana — like this lamp going out. In the Sangha this is the supreme jewel. By this truth may there be well-being."

Mangalasutta — Like the Mettasutta and the Ratanasutta, the auspicious recitation of this sutta is also considered to bring blessings.

A certain deity came to the Blessed One and said: "Desiring well-being, many devas and humans have reflected on what constitutes a blessing. Please tell us what the highest blessing is."

The Blessed One said: "Not to associate with fools, to associate with the wise, to honor those worthy of honor — this is the highest blessing. To live in a suitable place, to have done meritorious deeds before, to set oneself on the right path — this is the highest blessing. Great learning, skill in crafts, well-trained discipline, and well-spoken words — this is the highest blessing. To serve one's mother and father, to support one's wife and children, to engage in orderly work — this is the highest blessing. Generosity, righteous conduct, caring for relatives, blameless action — this is the highest blessing. To refrain from evil, to give up evil, abstinence from intoxicants, diligence in Dhamma — this is the highest blessing. To be respectful in conduct, to be free from pride, to be content, to be grateful, to listen to the Dhamma at the right time — this is the highest blessing. Patience, listening to others, visiting the virtuous, discussing the Dhamma at the right time — this is the highest blessing. Austerity, celibacy, seeing the Noble Truths, realizing Nirvana — this is the highest blessing. When touched by the vicissitudes of the world, one whose mind does not waver, who remains free from sorrow and passion — this is the highest blessing. By doing such things, one attains well-being everywhere; this indeed is their highest blessing."

Brahmanadhammikasutt — This sutta shows the virtues of the ancient brahmins and the faults of the modern ones. The reverence for cows is also affirmed. The Buddha says: "Like mother, father, brother, and other relatives, the cow is supremely beneficial to us. The cow gives food, strength, color, and happiness. When brahmins began sacrificing cows in their rituals, great misfortunes began to arise. Desire, hunger, and old age were formerly only three diseases. Due to cow-sacrifice, their number grew to ninety-eight."

(k) Determination of Textual Variants

In determining textual variants, along with considering the etymology and derivation of words, attention has also been paid to which forms have had the greatest historical prevalence. If a word has been found to have multiple forms established from both perspectives, we have placed one in the main text and the other in the footnote at the bottom of the page. In the footnotes, the symbols ro., si., sya., and ma. are used respectively for Roman, Sinhala, Siamese, and Maram (Burmese) editions.

5. The Discourse on Blessings

Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Savatthi, in the Jeta Grove, in the park of Anathapindika. Then, when the night was far advanced, a certain deity of surpassing beauty, illuminating the entire Jeta Grove, approached the Blessed One, and having approached and paid homage to him, stood to one side. Standing to one side, that deity addressed the Blessed One in verse:

1. Many gods and humans, longing for well-being, have pondered what blessings are. Tell us what the highest blessing is.

2. Not associating with fools, associating with the wise, and honoring those worthy of honor — this is the highest blessing.

3. Living in a suitable place, having made merit in the past, and having set oneself on the right path — this is the highest blessing.

4. Wide learning, and skill, well-trained discipline, and speech that is well-spoken — this is the highest blessing.

5. Supporting one's mother and father, caring for one's wife and children, and work that is free from conflict — this is the highest blessing.

6. Generosity, living by the Dhamma, caring for one's relatives, and blameless actions — this is the highest blessing.

7. Refraining and abstaining from evil, restraint from intoxicants, and diligence in the Dhamma — this is the highest blessing.

8. Respect and humility, contentment and gratitude, and listening to the Dhamma at the proper time — this is the highest blessing.

9. Patience and being open to correction, and seeing those who are wandering ascetics, and timely discussion of the Dhamma — this is the highest blessing.

10. Austerity and the holy life, seeing the noble truths, and the realization of Nibbana — this is the highest blessing.

6. The Jewel Discourse

1. Whatever beings have gathered here, whether on the earth or in the sky — may all beings be of happy mind, and may they also listen attentively to what is spoken.

3. Whatever treasure there may be here or beyond, or whatever precious jewel there is in the heavens — none of these is equal to the Tathagata. This too is a precious jewel in the Buddha. By this truth, may there be well-being.

4. The destruction of craving, dispassion, the deathless — the excellent state that Sakyamuni, composed in meditation, attained — nothing equals that Dhamma. This too is a precious jewel in the Dhamma. By this truth, may there be well-being.

          Summary of Chapters in the Dhammapada

The Pairs, Heedfulness, Mind, Flowers, the Fool and the Wise One — the Arahant, the Thousands, Evil, the Rod — these ten [chapters]. Old Age, Self, the World, the Buddha, Happiness, the Beloved — with the Path Chapter, twenty. Miscellaneous, Hell, the Elephant, Craving, the Monk, and the Brahmin — these twenty-six chapters were taught by the Kinsman of the Sun.

In the Pairs chapter, twenty verses; in Heedfulness, twelve. In the Mind chapter, eleven; in the Flowers chapter, sixteen. In the Fool chapter, sixteen verses; in the Wise One, fourteen. In the Arahant, ten verses; in the Thousands, sixteen. Thirteen in the Evil chapter; in the Rod, ten and seven. Eleven in the Old Age chapter; in the Self chapter, ten. Twelve in the World chapter; in the Buddha chapter, eighteen. In Happiness and the Beloved chapter, the verses are twelve.

1. The Chapter on Enlightenment

1. The First Sutta on Enlightenment

1. Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Uruvela, on the bank of the river Nerañjara, at the foot of the Bodhi tree, having just attained supreme enlightenment. At that time the Blessed One sat for seven days in one posture, experiencing the bliss of liberation. Then, when those seven days had passed, the Blessed One emerged from that concentration and during the first watch of the night carefully attended to dependent origination in forward order:

"When this exists, this comes to be; with the arising of this, this arises — namely: with ignorance as condition, formations; with formations as condition, consciousness; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases; with the six sense bases as condition, contact; with contact as condition, feeling; with feeling as condition, craving; with craving as condition, clinging; with clinging as condition, existence; with existence as condition, birth; with birth as condition, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair come into being. Such is the origin of this whole mass of suffering."

2. Then, having understood the meaning of this, the Blessed One on that occasion uttered this inspired utterance:

"When the truths become manifest
to the ardent meditating brahmin,
all his doubts then vanish away,
since he has come to know the law with its cause."

2. The Second Enlightenment Sutta

3. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Uruvela, on the bank of the river Neranjara, at the foot of the Bodhi tree, having just attained full enlightenment. At that time the Blessed One sat for seven days in a single cross-legged posture, experiencing the bliss of liberation. Then, after those seven days had passed, the Blessed One emerged from that meditation and in the middle watch of the night reflected carefully on dependent origination in reverse order:

"When this is not, that does not come to be; with the cessation of this, that ceases. That is: with the cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of formations; with the cessation of formations comes the cessation of consciousness; with the cessation of consciousness comes the cessation of name-and-form; with the cessation of name-and-form comes the cessation of the six sense bases; with the cessation of the six sense bases comes the cessation of contact; with the cessation of contact comes the cessation of feeling; with the cessation of feeling comes the cessation of craving; with the cessation of craving comes the cessation of clinging; with the cessation of clinging comes the cessation of becoming; with the cessation of becoming comes the cessation of birth; with the cessation of birth, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease. Such is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering."

4. Then, having understood this matter, the Blessed One at that moment uttered this inspired utterance:

"When phenomena become manifest
to the ardently meditating brahmin,
all his doubts then vanish,
since he has come to know the destruction of conditions."

3. The Third Enlightenment Sutta

5. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Uruvela, on the bank of the river Neranjara, at the foot of the Bodhi tree, having just attained full enlightenment. At that time the Blessed One sat for seven days in a single cross-legged posture, experiencing the bliss of liberation. "Thus, when this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises. When this does not exist, that does not come to be; with the cessation of this, that ceases. That is to say —
From ignorance as condition arise formations; from formations as condition arises consciousness; from consciousness as condition arises name-and-form; from name-and-form as condition arise the six sense bases; from the six sense bases as condition arises contact; from contact as condition arises feeling; from feeling as condition arises craving; from craving as condition arises clinging; from clinging as condition arises becoming; from becoming as condition arises birth; from birth as condition arise aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. Such is the arising of this entire mass of suffering.

"But with the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of formations; with the cessation of formations, the cessation of consciousness; with the cessation of consciousness, the cessation of name-and-form; with the cessation of name-and-form, the cessation of the six sense bases; with the cessation of the six sense bases, the cessation of contact; with the cessation of contact, the cessation of feeling; with the cessation of feeling, the cessation of craving; with the cessation of craving, the cessation of clinging; with the cessation of clinging, the cessation of becoming; with the cessation of becoming, the cessation of birth; with the cessation of birth, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease. Such is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering."

1. The Mucalinda Sutta

1. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Uruvelā on the bank of the river Nerañjarā, at the foot of the Mucalinda tree, having just attained full enlightenment. At that time the Blessed One sat for seven days in a single cross-legged posture, experiencing the bliss of liberation.

Now at that time a great unseasonal storm arose, lasting seven days, with rain, cold wind, and dark skies. Then Mucalinda the Nāga king came out from his dwelling and, having encircled the Blessed One's body seven times with his coils, stood spreading his great hood above his head, thinking: "Let not the Blessed One be cold, let not the Blessed One be hot, let not the Blessed One be touched by flies, mosquitoes, wind, heat, or creeping things."

Then, when seven days had passed, the Blessed One emerged from that meditative absorption. Mucalinda the Nāga king, knowing that the sky was clear and free of clouds, unwound his coils from the Blessed One's body, withdrew his own form, and taking on the appearance of a young man, stood before the Blessed One with hands joined in reverence, paying homage to him.

2. Then the Blessed One, understanding the meaning of this, on that occasion uttered this inspired utterance:

"Happy is seclusion for one who is content, who has heard the Dhamma and sees clearly.
Happy is non-affliction in the world, restraint toward living beings.
Happy is dispassion in the world, the overcoming of sensual desires.
But the removal of the conceit 'I am' — that indeed is the supreme happiness."

24. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Uruvela, on the bank of the Neranjara river, at the foot of the Bodhi tree, just newly enlightened. At that time the Blessed One was seated in one cross-legged posture for seven days, experiencing the bliss of liberation.

"This world has arisen in suffering,
Beset by contact, it speaks of disease as self.
Whatever it conceives of,
That turns out to be otherwise.
The world, subject to change, is attached to becoming,
Overcome by becoming, it delights in becoming itself.
What it delights in is fear,
What it fears is suffering.
This holy life is lived for the abandoning of becoming.

1. The First Sutta Connected with Nibbana

1. Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Savatthi, in the Jeta Grove, in the monastery of Anathapindika. At that time the Blessed One was instructing, urging, rousing, and gladdening the monks with a Dhamma talk connected with Nibbana. Those monks, taking it to heart, applying their minds, gathering all their attention, were listening to the Dhamma with open ears.

2. Then the Blessed One, understanding the significance of this, on that occasion uttered this solemn utterance:

"There is, monks, that sphere where there is neither earth, nor water, nor fire, nor air; neither the sphere of infinite space, nor the sphere of infinite consciousness, nor the sphere of nothingness, nor the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; neither this world nor another world, nor both; neither moon nor sun. There, monks, I say, there is neither coming nor going, nor standing still, nor arising, nor passing away. It is without foundation, without continuance, without a footing. This, truly, is the end of suffering."

1. The Discourse on Greed

1. This was said by the Blessed One, said by the Arahant — thus have I heard:
"Abandon one thing, monks; I am your guarantor for non-return. What is that one thing? Abandon greed, monks — that one thing; I am your guarantor for non-return." This was the meaning spoken by the Blessed One. Concerning this, it is said:

"Beings who are overcome by greed go to a bad destination.
Having rightly understood that greed, those who see clearly abandon it.

8. Sutta on Full Understanding of Conceit

8. This was said by the Blessed One, said by the Arahant — so I have heard:
"Monks, one who does not directly know and fully understand conceit, who has not dispassioned the mind toward it, who has not abandoned it, is incapable of the destruction of suffering. "This population is possessed by conceit, bound by conceit, delighting in becoming.
Not fully understanding conceit, they come back again and again to renewed existence.

they, having overcome the fetter of conceit, have transcended all suffering."

22. Mettasutta

22. This was said by the Blessed One, said by the Arahant — thus have I heard:

"Monks, do not fear merit. This word 'merit' is a name for happiness, for what is wished for, desired, agreeable, and pleasing. I recall, monks, that having done merit over a long time, I experienced for a long time what is wished for, desired, agreeable, and pleasing. Having developed a mind of loving-kindness for seven years, I did not return to this world for seven aeons of contraction and expansion. When the aeon was contracting, monks, I went to the realm of the Streaming Radiance (Abhassara); when it was expanding, I was reborn in an empty Brahma mansion. There, monks, I was Brahma, the Great Brahma, the Unconquered, the All-seeing, the Sovereign. Thirty-six times, monks, I was Sakka, lord of the gods; countless times I was a wheel-turning king, righteous, a righteous king, ruler of the four quarters, conqueror, possessor of the seven treasures. What need is there to speak of local kingship!

"To me, monks, this thought arose: 'What is the fruit of this kamma, what is the result of this kamma, by which I am now of such great power and such great majesty?' Then it occurred to me: 'This is the fruit of three kammas, the result of three kammas, by which I am now of such great power and such great majesty — namely, giving, self-control, and restraint.'" The Blessed One spoke this meaning. There it is said:

"One should practice merit, which brings future happiness.
One should cultivate giving, a life of harmony, and a mind of loving-kindness.

26. Dana Sutta (Discourse on Giving)

26. This was said by the Blessed One, said by the Arahant — so I have heard:
"Monks, if beings knew, as I know, the fruit of sharing gifts, they would not eat without having given, nor would the stain of miserliness take hold of their minds. Even if it were their last morsel, their last mouthful, they would not eat without sharing it, if there were someone to receive it. But because, monks, beings do not know the fruit of sharing gifts as I know it, they eat without giving, and the stain of miserliness takes hold of their minds." what great fruit comes from sharing gifts —

they would give in due season to the noble ones, where giving bears great fruit.
Having given food in abundance, offering to those worthy of offerings,
those who depart from here as humans go to heaven as donors.
Having gone to heaven, there they rejoice, enjoying what they desire.

2. The Book of Twos

1. Sutta on Living in Suffering

1. Two things were spoken of without being called forth — this was said by the Blessed One, said by the Accomplished One — thus have I heard:

"Monks, a monk endowed with two things lives, in this very life, in suffering, with distress, anguish, and fever; and at the breaking up of the body after death, a bad destination is to be expected. What are the two? Not guarding the doors of the sense faculties, and lack of moderation in eating. Monks, a monk endowed with these two things lives, in this very life, in suffering, with distress, anguish, and fever; and at the breaking up of the body after death, a bad destination is to be expected."

The Blessed One spoke this meaning. Concerning this it is said:

"Eye, ear, and nose, tongue, body, and likewise mind —
these are the doors of one whose faculties are unguarded, O monk.

Without moderation in food, unrestrained in the sense faculties,
he encounters bodily suffering and mental suffering.

With body burning, with mind burning,
whether by day or by night, such a one lives in suffering."

This meaning too was spoken by the Blessed One — thus have I heard.

15. This was said by the Blessed One, said by the Arahant — so I have heard:

3. THE BOOK OF THREES

1. The Root Sutta

1. This was said by the Blessed One, said by the Arahant — thus have I heard:
"There are three roots of the unwholesome, monks. What are the three? Greed is a root of the unwholesome, hatred is a root of the unwholesome, delusion is a root of the unwholesome — these, monks, are the three roots of the unwholesome." This is the meaning the Blessed One spoke. On this it is said:

"Greed and hatred and delusion — these arise from within oneself and destroy a person of evil mind, as a reed is destroyed by its own fruit."

This meaning too was spoken by the Blessed One — thus have I heard.

2. The Elements Sutta

2. This was said by the Blessed One, said by the Arahant — thus have I heard:
"There are three elements, monks. What are the three? The form element, the formless element, the cessation element — these, monks, are the three elements." This is the meaning the Blessed One spoke. On this it is said:

"Having fully understood the form element, not settling in the formless realms,
those who are liberated in cessation — those people are ones who have abandoned death.
Having touched with the body the deathless element, free from acquisitions,
having realized the relinquishment of acquisitions, free from taints,
the Perfectly Enlightened One teaches the sorrowless, stainless state."

This meaning too was spoken by the Blessed One — thus have I heard.

3. First Discourse on Feeling

3. This was said by the Blessed One, said by the Arahant — so I have heard:

"Monks, there are three feelings. What are the three? Pleasant feeling, painful feeling, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling — these, monks, are the three feelings." The Blessed One spoke this meaning. In reference to it, this is said:

"The concentrated, clearly comprehending disciple of the Buddha, who is mindful,
understands feelings and their arising.
Where they cease, and the path leading to their ending —
by the ending of feelings, the monk is without hunger, fully quenched."

This meaning too was spoken by the Blessed One — so I have heard.

4. Second Discourse on Feeling

4. This was said by the Blessed One, said by the Arahant — so I have heard:

"Monks, there are three feelings. What are the three? Pleasant feeling, painful feeling, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. Pleasant feeling, monks, is to be seen as painful; painful feeling is to be seen as a dart; neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is to be seen as impermanent. When, monks, a monk has seen pleasant feeling as painful, painful feeling as a dart, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling as impermanent — he is called, monks, 'a monk who is a noble one with right vision, who has cut off craving, removed the fetter, and by rightly comprehending conceit has made an end of suffering.'" The Blessed One spoke this meaning. In reference to it, this is said:

"One who has seen pleasure as painful, pain as a dart,
and has seen the peaceful neither-painful-nor-pleasant as impermanent —
that monk, a right seer, is thereby liberated from it.
Stilled, with full knowledge, he has gone beyond attachment — he is a sage."

This meaning too was spoken by the Blessed One — so I have heard.

5. This was said by the Blessed One, said by the Arahant — thus have I heard:

This was said by the Blessed One. In reference to this, it is said:

"The disciple of the Buddha, composed, clearly comprehending, and mindful,
knows the searches and the origin of the searches.
Where they cease, and the path leading to their ending —
by the ending of searches, the monk, desireless, is fully quenched."

This meaning too was spoken by the Blessed One — thus have I heard.

6. Second Esanā Sutta

6. This was said by the Blessed One, said by the Arahant — thus have I heard:

"Monks, there are three searches. What are the three? The search for sensual pleasure, the search for existence, the search for the holy life — these, monks, are the three searches."

This was said by the Blessed One. In reference to this, it is said:

"The search for sensual pleasure, the search for existence, together with the search for the holy life —
these constitute adherence to views, and are the bases for the arising of wrong views.
One who is free from all passion, liberated through the destruction of craving,
has abandoned the searches, has uprooted the bases of views.
By the ending of searches, that monk is without longing, free from doubt."

This meaning too was spoken by the Blessed One — thus have I heard.

This was said by the Blessed One. In reference to this, it is said:

9. The Discourse on Craving

9. This was said by the Blessed One, said by the Arahant — so have I heard:
"Monks, there are three cravings. What are the three? Craving for sensual pleasure, craving for existence, craving for non-existence — these, monks, are the three cravings." Thus.
