27. The Discourse on the Wish for Happiness

27. This was said by the Blessed One, said by the Arahant — so I have heard:

"Monks, a wise person who wishes for three kinds of happiness should guard his virtue. What are the three? 'May praise come to me' — so thinking, a wise person should guard his virtue. 'May wealth arise for me' — so thinking, a wise person should guard his virtue. 'After the breaking up of the body at death, may I be reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world' — so thinking, a wise person should guard his virtue. Monks, wishing for these three kinds of happiness, a wise person should guard his virtue." This was the meaning spoken by the Blessed One. With regard to this, it is said:

"The wise person, seeking three kinds of happiness, should guard his virtue:
praise, acquisition of wealth, and rejoicing in heaven after death.

"Even one who does not do evil himself, but associates with one who does,
becomes suspect in regard to evil, and his ill-repute grows.

"Whatever kind of friend one makes, whatever kind one associates with,
one becomes like that — for companionship makes one similar.

"One who mingles with those who mingle, touched by contact with another,
like an arrow in a quiver rubbing against others, becomes smeared by what is unsmeared.
Fearing such contamination, the wise person should not befriend the wicked.

"Just as one who wraps putrid fish in grass — the grass too takes on the stench —
so it is with associating with the foolish.

"But just as one who wraps fragrant tagara wood in leaves — the leaves too take on the fragrance —
so it is with associating with the wise.

"Therefore, knowing one's own ripening as a leaf-cup, a wise person should not associate with the bad but should associate with the good.
The bad lead one to hell; the good bring one to a happy destination."

This too was spoken by the Blessed One — so I have heard.

42. This was said by the Blessed One, said by the Arahant — so I have heard:

"Monks, overcome and obsessed by three unwholesome qualities, Devadatta has gone to a place of loss, to hell, remaining there for an eon, beyond cure. By what three? 41. Aggappasāda Sutta (The Discourse on the Highest Confidence)

The Book of Fours is concluded.

Its Udana (summary verse):

The knower easy for brahmins, the conduct of ascetics, craving, Brahma,
The greatly beneficial, the deceivers, the one who wanders accomplished — thirteen in all.

*Sutta Collection Summary

The section of twenty-seven, the pair, the collection of twenty-two suttas,
The group of fifty, and thirteen and the fours — this is what it amounts to.
In two hundred and twelve suttas, the arahants of old compiled and gathered them,
For their lasting preservation — that is what is called the Itivuttaka.
The Itivuttaka Pali is concluded.

At that time, about five hundred ploughs of the brahmin Kasibharadvaja were harnessed at the sowing season. Then the Blessed One, having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl and robe, approached the place where the brahmin Kasibharadvaja was working. At that time —

At that time the serving of food was taking place at the brahmin Kasibharadvaja's house. Then the Blessed One approached where the serving was going on; having approached, he stood to one side.

The brahmin Kasibharadvaja saw the Blessed One standing for alms. Having seen him, he said to the Blessed One: "I, O ascetic, plow and I sow; having plowed and sown, I eat. You too, O ascetic, should plow and sow; having plowed and sown, eat."

"I too, O brahmin, plow and sow; having plowed and sown, I eat."

"But we do not see the good Gotama's yoke, or plow, or plowshare, or goad, or oxen; yet the good Gotama says: 'I too, O brahmin, plow and sow; having plowed and sown, I eat.'"

Then the brahmin Kasibharadvaja addressed the Blessed One in verse:

"Then to whom, venerable Gotama, shall I give this rice-milk?"

"I do not see, O brahmin, in the world with its gods, its Maras, and its Brahmas, with its population of ascetics and brahmins, gods and humans, anyone for whom, if this rice-milk were eaten, it would be properly digested — except for a Tathagata or a disciple of a Tathagata. Just as a plowshare heated all day, when dropped into water, sizzles and hisses, steams and smokes — in exactly the same way, that rice-milk, when dropped into the water, sizzled and hissed, steamed and smoked.

                    7. The Vasala Sutta (Discourse on the Outcast)

Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Savatthi, in the Jetavana monastery of Anathapindika. Then the Blessed One, having dressed in the morning and taken his robe and bowl, entered Savatthi for alms. At that time, in the house of the brahmin Aggikabharadvaja, a fire had been kindled and an oblation was being offered. Then the Blessed One, going through Savatthi for alms house by house, approached the dwelling of the brahmin Aggikabharadvaja.

The brahmin Aggikabharadvaja saw the Blessed One coming from afar. Seeing him, he said to the Blessed One: "Stay right there, you shaveling; stay right there, you miserable ascetic; stay right there, you outcast — just stay there!"

When this was said, the Blessed One spoke to the brahmin Aggikabharadvaja: "Do you know, brahmin, what an outcast is, or the things that make one an outcast?"

"No indeed, good Gotama, I do not know what an outcast is, or the things that make one an outcast. It would be good if the venerable Gotama would teach me the Dhamma in such a way that I might come to know what an outcast is, or the things that make one an outcast." 2. The Minor Collection

1. The Jewel Discourse

1. Whatever beings have gathered here,
Whether on earth or in the sky above —
May all beings be joyful in heart,
And listen with care to what is spoken.

2. Therefore, all you beings, pay heed,
Show loving-kindness to the human race.
Day and night they bring offerings to you,
So guard them well, with diligence.

3. Whatever treasure there is here or beyond,
Or whatever precious jewel exists in the heavens —
None is equal to the Tathagata.
This precious jewel is in the Buddha.
By this truth, may there be well-being.

4. The extinction, the freedom from passion, the deathless, the excellent —
That which the Sakyan sage, composed, attained —
There is nothing equal to that Dhamma.
This precious jewel is in the Dhamma.
By this truth, may there be well-being.

5. What the most excellent Buddha praised as pure —
The concentration called "immediate" —
No concentration is equal to that.
This precious jewel is in the Dhamma.
By this truth, may there be well-being.

7. The Brahmin Dhamma Sutta

Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was residing at Savatthi, in the Jetavana grove of Anathapindika. Then many Kosalan brahmin householders — aged, elderly, advanced in years, who had lived long and reached the end of their lives — approached the Blessed One; having approached, they exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. Having exchanged pleasant and courteous words, they sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, those brahmin householders said to the Blessed One: "Are there now, Master Gotama, brahmins who follow the brahmin dhamma of the ancient brahmins?"

"No, brahmins, there are not now brahmins who follow the brahmin dhamma of the ancient brahmins."

"It would be good, Master Gotama, if the venerable Gotama would speak about the brahmin dhamma of the ancient brahmins, if it is not too much trouble for the venerable Gotama."

"Well then, brahmins, listen carefully and pay attention; I shall speak." "Yes, sir," those brahmin householders replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said:

4. Sundarikabharadvaja Sutta

Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling among the Kosalans on the bank of the Sundarika river. At that very time the brahmin Sundarikabharadvaja was making fire-offerings on the bank of the Sundarika river, tending the sacred fire. Then the brahmin Sundarikabharadvaja, having made the fire-offering and tended the sacred fire, rose from his seat and looked around in all four directions, thinking: "Who now might enjoy the remains of this oblation?" The brahmin Sundarikabharadvaja saw the Blessed One seated not far away at the root of a certain tree, head wrapped and covered. Seeing him, he took the remains of the oblation in his left hand and his water-pot in his right hand, and approached the Blessed One.

Then the Blessed One, hearing the sound of the brahmin Sundarikabharadvaja's footsteps, uncovered his head. Then the brahmin Sundarikabharadvaja, thinking "This person is shaven-headed, this one is a shaveling," was on the point of turning back right there. But then it occurred to the brahmin Sundarikabharadvaja: "Some brahmins here too are indeed shaven-headed — let me approach and ask about his birth." So the brahmin Sundarikabharadvaja approached the Blessed One; having approached, he said to the Blessed One: "Of what birth is the venerable one?"

At that time, certain questions had arisen in the mind of the wanderer Sabhiya, posed by a deity who had formerly been his blood relative: "Sabhiya, whichever ascetic or brahmin answers these questions of yours — in his presence you should lead the holy life."

7. Sela-sutta

Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was wandering on tour among the Anguttarapas with a large community of monks, with twelve hundred and fifty monks, and he arrived at a market town of the Anguttarapas called Apana. Keniya the matted-hair ascetic heard: "The recluse Gotama, the son of the Sakyans, who went forth from the Sakyan clan, is wandering on tour among the Anguttarapas with a large community of monks, with twelve hundred and fifty monks, and has arrived at Apana. And this good report has spread concerning that venerable Gotama: 'Such indeed is the Blessed One — he is an arahant, a fully enlightened one, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, a fortunate one, a knower of the world, unsurpassed trainer of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One.' He proclaims this world with its gods, its Maras, its Brahmas, with its community of recluses and brahmins, its gods and humans, having realized it by his own direct knowledge. He teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with meaning and phrasing, complete and perfectly pure, the holy life he reveals. Truly, to see such arahants is good."

Then Keniya the matted-hair ascetic approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. Having exchanged pleasant and courteous greetings, he sat down to one side. To Keniya the matted-hair ascetic, sitting to one side, the Blessed One gave a teaching, an exhortation, an encouragement, and an inspiration by means of a talk on the Dhamma. Then Keniya the matted-hair ascetic, having been taught, exhorted, encouraged, and inspired by the Blessed One's talk on the Dhamma, said to the Blessed One: "May the venerable Gotama consent to accept tomorrow's meal together with the community of monks." When this was said, the Blessed One replied to Keniya the matted-hair ascetic: "The community of monks is large, Keniya — twelve hundred and fifty monks — and you are devoted to the brahmins."

173. The life of mortals here is without sign, without certainty — it is hard, brief, and bound up with suffering.

174. There is no means by which those who are born do not die. Having reached old age, there is death — this is the nature of living beings.

9. The Vasettha Sutta

Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Icchananagala, in the Icchananagala forest grove. At that time many well-known and greatly renowned brahmin householders were residing at Icchananagala — namely, Canki the brahmin, Tarukkha the brahmin, Pokkharasati the brahmin, Jannussoni the brahmin, Todeyya the brahmin, and other well-known and greatly renowned brahmin householders. Then, as the young men Vasettha and Bharadvaja were walking back and forth and wandering about, this conversation arose between them: "How, friend, does one become a brahmin?"

The young man Bharadvaja said: "When, friend, one is well-born on both sides — from the mother's side and from the father's side — of pure descent back to the seventh generation of ancestors, not reproached or censured in terms of birth — to that extent, friend, one is a brahmin."

The young man Vasettha said: "When, friend, one is virtuous and accomplished in conduct — to that extent, friend, one is a brahmin." Now the young man Bharadvaja was unable to convince the young man Vasettha, and the young man Vasettha was unable to convince the young man Bharadvaja.

10. The Kokālika Sutta

Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was staying at Savatthi, in Jeta's Grove, in the park of Anathapindika. Then the monk Kokalika approached the Blessed One, paid his respects, sat down to one side, and said to him: "Venerable sir, Sariputta and Moggallana have evil wishes; they have fallen under the sway of evil desires."

Then Brahma Sahampati, as the night was waning, of surpassing radiance, illuminating the entire Jetavana, approached where the Blessed One was; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he stood to one side. 12. The Discourse on Contemplation of Pairs

Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Savatthi, in the Eastern Park, in the Palace of Migara's Mother. On that occasion, on the Uposatha day of the fifteenth, on the night of the full moon, the Blessed One was seated in the open air, surrounded by the community of monks. Then the Blessed One, having surveyed the community of monks sitting in silence, addressed the monks:

"If, monks, someone were to ask: 'What is the basis for hearing those skillful teachings that are noble, leading out, and conducive to full awakening?' — they should be told: 'Precisely for the sake of understanding, as it truly is, the pair of things.' And what is the pair that you speak of?

(1) 'This is suffering, this is the origin of suffering' — this is one contemplation. 'This is the cessation of suffering, this is the path leading to the cessation of suffering' — this is the second contemplation. Thus, monks, a monk who correctly contemplates pairs, dwelling ardent, clearly comprehending, and resolute, can expect one of two fruits: either final knowledge right here in this very life, or, if there is a remainder of clinging, non-return.

The Blessed One said this. Having said this, the Well-Gone One, the Teacher, further said:

323. "Those who do not understand suffering, nor its arising,
nor where all suffering completely ceases without remainder,
nor do they know the path that leads to the stilling of suffering —

324. They are lacking in liberation of mind and liberation through wisdom;
they are incapable of making an end; they go on subject to birth and aging.

325. But those who do understand suffering, and its arising,
and where all suffering completely ceases without remainder,
and who know the path that leads to the stilling of suffering —

8. The Atthakavagga

1. The Discourse on Sensual Pleasures

1. For one who desires a sensual object, if that desire is fulfilled,
he is surely glad at heart — the mortal gains what he wished for.

2. But for that being, filled with longing and desire,
if those pleasures diminish, he suffers as if struck by an arrow.

3. One who avoids sensual pleasures, as one avoids a snake's head with one's foot,
mindfully passes beyond this clinging attachment to the world.

4. Fields, property, gold, cattle and servants,
women, relatives, many sensual pleasures — whoever craves these things,

5. weaknesses overpower him, troubles overwhelm him who is intoxicated,
and then suffering follows him, as water floods a broken boat.

6. Therefore, let a being always be mindful, avoiding sensual pleasures.
Abandoning them, cross the flood — as one who has bailed out a boat reaches the far shore.

2. The Discourse on the Cave

7. Attached, dwelling in the cave, covered over by much,
a person standing firm in delusion.
One such as this is far from seclusion —
for sensual pleasures in the world are not easily abandoned.

8. Bound to existence by the root of craving,
they are hard to release, not easily freed.

5. The Pārāyana Chapter

1. The Background Verses

1. From the pleasant city of Kosala he journeyed to the southern region, that brahmin who was master of sacred texts, seeking the state of nothingness.

2. In the territory of Assaka, near Alaka, he dwelt on the bank of the Godhāvarī river, living on gleaned grain and fruit.

3. Close by his hermitage there arose a large village, and with the income generated from it he prepared a great sacrifice.

4. Having performed the great sacrifice, he returned again to his hermitage. When he had re-entered it, another brahmin came.

5. Feet swollen, thirsty, with dust-covered teeth and head, he approached him and asked for five hundred coins.

6. Seeing that brahmin, Bāvarī invited him to a seat, asked after his welfare and happiness, and then spoke these words:

7. "Whatever gift it was mine to give, all of it has already been distributed by me. Forgive me, friend, I do not have five hundred."

8. "If you, being asked, do not provide what I need, then on the seventh day may your head split into seven pieces."

9. That fraud, having uttered this fearful curse, departed. Hearing those words, Bāvarī became deeply distressed.

10. Not eating, he grew thin, pierced by the dart of grief, and his mind, in such a state, found no joy even in meditation.
